title: Why a Crossed-Out Price Makes a Deal Look Bigger
h1: Why a crossed-out Black Friday price makes a deal look bigger than it is
question: If a Black Friday deal shows a higher price struck through, is that the price the item really cost before the sale?
answer: Not always. A Groundwork Collaborative report found that 29.1% of the products Amazon featured as Black Friday and Cyber Monday deals in 2024 and 2025 cost the same or more than their lowest price in the previous 30 days. Amazon calls it "deeply flawed and false". Either way, you judge the saving from the crossed-out number.

event.name: The Groundwork Collaborative's report "Deal or Decoy? Amazon's Deceptive Discounts", ahead of Black Friday on 27 November 2026

artefact.text: The report compares the prices of 351 products from Amazon's Black Friday and Cyber Monday deals pages in 2024 and 2025 with each product's lowest price in the 30 days before, using price history from Keepa.
artefact.label: Read the report

timeline.text: The Groundwork Collaborative publishes "Deal or Decoy? Amazon's Deceptive Discounts". It finds "nearly 1 in 3 (29.1%) had a sale event price that was the same or higher than the lowest price in the 30 days".
Amazon responds in a statement, calling the claims "deeply flawed and false" and saying it is tightening the rules for upcoming sales.
Digital Trends reports the study and Amazon's answer, and explains where Amazon says a crossed-out list price comes from.
Black Friday 2026, the day after US Thanksgiving.

mechanism.text: On Amazon's sale event pages, Groundwork describes "a sale event price next to a struckthrough "list price" or "typical price,"". One product page it shows had "a struckthrough "list price" of $64.99, a lower "deal price" of $24.99 right above it". The shopper meets two numbers, and the bigger one is presented as the starting point.

mechanism.h: The saving is judged from that number
mechanism.text: The anchoring effect is that the first number you meet drags your estimate toward it. Here the estimate is what the item is worth, or how good the price is. Set against $64.99, $24.99 reads as a large cut. Nothing on the display tells you whether $64.99 is a price anyone recently paid.

mechanism.h: The anchor need not be a recent price
mechanism.text: According to Digital Trends, Amazon says "a crossed-out list price can be a manufacturer's suggested price" "or a price Amazon or another retailer charged as far back as 90 to 180 days". So the anchor can sit well above what the product cost last week, and the deal is judged against the anchor, not against last week.

mechanism.h: Where the anchor and the recent price part ways
mechanism.text: Groundwork measured against a different reference, the lowest price in the prior 30 days. By that measure, "roughly 9% had a sale event price that was higher than the lowest price of the product". Its examples include a pair of Hunter women's short rain boots "on sale" for $126.99 on Black Friday 2025 that "had been $79.97 just nine days before the sale event started". A saving that looks real from the struck-through price can be a rise from the recent one.

Digital Trends notes that "The European Union requires a seller advertising a discount to show its own lowest price from the prior 30 days" and that "The US has no comparable federal rule." Groundwork recommends that "policymakers should require retailers to disclose the lowest price the product has sold for in the previous 30 days." In anchoring terms, both put a more relevant first number in front of the buyer.

limits: Nobody in this story measured shoppers. The report measures prices, not judgements. That the struck-through price shifts what buyers think a deal is worth is our reading through the anchoring effect, not a finding of the report.

Amazon disputes the analysis. It says "350 items are a tiny fraction of the over 10m deals available" and that "98% of the products were at the same price or lower than the price over the prior 30 days", and that some earlier lows were Early Event deals. Groundwork says all the products came from Amazon's sale event pages.

The data covers Black Friday and Cyber Monday in 2024 and 2025, not 2026. Amazon says it is tightening the rules so event deals "will almost always be better than the prior 30-day low", and we have not seen any check of this year's deals.
For the boots and the other examples, the report gives the sale price and the earlier price. We did not see which struck-through price, if any, was displayed next to each one.
A deal badge alone can mislead without any number to anchor on. Part of what the report describes may be that, rather than anchoring.

faqs.q: So are Amazon's Black Friday deals fake?
faqs.a: The report does not say that. It says about 29% of the featured deals it checked in 2024 and 2025 were no cheaper than their 30-day low, and roughly 9% were dearer. Amazon says 98% of the products were at or below their prior 30-day price. The two sides disagree on the data.

faqs.q: How can I check a deal myself?
faqs.a: Look at the price history rather than the struck-through price. Digital Trends notes that "Keepa and CamelCamelCamel offer free charts of the same data", and Amazon says Alexa can show a year of price history.

faqs.q: Is it legal to show a crossed-out price the item hasn't sold at recently?
faqs.a: It depends where. In the EU a seller advertising a discount has to show its own lowest price from the prior 30 days. Digital Trends reports that the US has no comparable federal rule.

predictions.text: Amazon said it is tightening its rules so event deals will almost always be better than the prior 30-day low. By 31 January 2027, a published price-history check of Amazon's Black Friday or Cyber Monday 2026 featured deals finds fewer than 1 in 10 no cheaper than their 30-day low. If such a check finds 1 in 10 or more, this was wrong.

actions: Before you judge a deal, find the lowest price the item sold at in the last month, and measure the saving from that, not from the crossed-out number.
Treat a struck-through "list price" as a number someone chose to show you first.
Read the report and Amazon's reply together. They disagree, and both are on the record.
whyItMatters: A crossed-out price is the anchoring effect built into a shop display. This report shows how far that first number can sit from what an item recently cost, and why rules that require the 30-day low change what a buyer measures the saving against.
